Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
The world is a dangerous place
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

vignette: Señor García is a 67-year-old widowed prosecutor who has been struggling with the aftermath of a sexual assault that occurred two years ago. The event left him profoundly shaken and has significantly impacted his daily life. Señor García’s trauma began when he was assaulted in a public park late at night by someone known to him, an acquaintance from work. This intimate violation made being around familiar faces particularly triggering for him, especially if children were present, as it reminded him of the vulnerability associated with such situations. Señor García vividly recalls every detail of the assault—the cold chill that settled on his skin, the fear and helplessness he felt, and how acutely aware he was of every sound and movement around him. This vividness is so intense that the memory feels present rather than past, as though it continues to unfold right now. For instance, when Señor García sees children playing in a park or any known person from his work, these scenes instantly transport him back to that night, making the assault feel current and immediate. The memory’s uncontrolled access has made life increasingly difficult for Señor García. He avoids going to unfamiliar places because he cannot assess potential dangers adequately. This avoidance is compounded by his constant scanning of exits whenever he enters any room or building. The mere presence of a specific temperature on his skin, reminiscent of that cold night, triggers these vivid memories and intensifies his sense of vulnerability. What frightens Señor García most are the thoughts that his body has been permanently damaged by what happened, and he feels dirty or contaminated as a result. This contamination belief is so pervasive that it influences how he interacts with others and perceives the world around him. He believes that the world is inherently dangerous, and this belief exacerbates his sense of threat. For instance, while at work prosecuting cases, Señor García constantly scans for potential weapons or any objects that could pose a risk, reinforcing his conviction that the environment is not safe. The contamination he feels also leads to an obsessive avoidance of certain people and places. He finds it increasingly challenging to attend social gatherings or even go to familiar locales where he might encounter known individuals or see children playing. These triggers fuel his vivid memories, which in turn exacerbate his negative appraisals about the world being dangerous and himself being permanently damaged. Señor García’s avoidance behaviors have had significant consequences. His work as a prosecutor has become particularly arduous because of the constant threat he perceives, leading to missed court dates and increased stress at his job. Additionally, his social life has diminished significantly; he avoids gatherings with friends and family out of fear that these settings might trigger intrusive memories or negative appraisals. Despite his efforts to manage his symptoms, Señor García's condition has worsened over time. The tight loop of triggers, vivid memories, negative appraisals, and heightened threat perception has created a self-reinforcing cycle where each element amplifies the others. He finally decided to seek help because he was struggling with basic tasks at work and in his daily life, realizing that his symptoms were interfering too much with his ability to function effectively. Señor García hopes that through therapy, he can regain control over his memories and reduce his sense of contamination and vulnerability. His primary fear is being unable to protect himself from further harm or experiencing another traumatic event, which underscores the urgency in seeking professional help.
